My Town and Local Area

This lesson covers AQA Theme 3: The environment and where people live — specifically describing your town, what there is to do, and comparing different areas. You need to use man kann (you can / one can), give opinions, and make comparisons. This topic links to the holiday and environment topics, so vocabulary overlaps.

Describing Your Town

Start with the basics — where you live and what your town is like:

Ich wohne in einer kleinen Stadt in Nordengland. — I live in a small town in the north of England.
Ich wohne in einem Dorf auf dem Land. — I live in a village in the countryside.
Ich wohne in einer Großstadt. — I live in a big city.
Ich wohne am Stadtrand. — I live on the outskirts.
Ich wohne in der Stadtmitte / im Stadtzentrum. — I live in the town centre.

die Geschäfte (pl) — shops
das Einkaufszentrum — shopping centre
das Kino — cinema
das Theater — theatre
das Schwimmbad / die Schwimmhalle — swimming pool
der Sportplatz — sports ground
das Sportzentrum — sports centre
der Park — park
die Bibliothek — library
das Museum — museum
das Restaurant — restaurant
das Café — café
die Kirche — church
der Markt — market
der Bahnhof — train station
die Bushaltestelle — bus stop

Key Fact

Use es gibt + accusative to say what there is in your town: Es gibt ein Kino, viele Geschäfte und einen schönen Park. (There is a cinema, many shops and a nice park.) To say what there isn’t: Es gibt kein Schwimmbad. (There is no swimming pool.)

What You Can Do — man kann

The impersonal man (one/you) + kann (can) is a key structure for describing activities in your area:

In meiner Stadt kann man viel machen. — In my town you can do a lot.
Man kann ins Kino gehen. — You can go to the cinema.
Man kann im Park spazieren gehen. — You can go for a walk in the park.
Man kann die Museen besuchen. — You can visit the museums.
Man kann einkaufen gehen. — You can go shopping.
Man kann im Sportzentrum Sport treiben. — You can do sport at the sports centre.

lebhaft/lebendig — lively
ruhig — quiet
langweilig — boring
schön — beautiful
hässlich — ugly
historisch — historic
modern — modern
industriell — industrial
touristisch — touristy
sauber — clean
schmutzig — dirty
sicher — safe
gefährlich — dangerous

Opinions About Where You Live

Give opinions with reasons to access higher marks:

Ich wohne gern hier, weil es viel zu tun gibt. — I like living here because there is a lot to do.
Ich finde meine Stadt langweilig, weil es nichts für junge Leute gibt. — I find my town boring because there is nothing for young people.
Das Beste an meiner Stadt ist der Park. — The best thing about my town is the park.
Es gefällt mir, dass es so ruhig ist. — I like that it is so quiet.
Es nervt mich, dass es keinen Bahnhof gibt. — It annoys me that there is no station.

Comparing Areas — Comparatives

The exam often asks you to compare town and country life, or compare your area with another place. You need Komparativ (comparative) forms:

To form the comparative, add -er to the adjective. Short adjectives often add an umlaut: groß → größer, alt → älter, klein → kleiner. Then use als (than):

Die Stadt ist größer als das Dorf. — The city is bigger than the village.
Das Dorf ist ruhiger als die Stadt. — The village is quieter than the city.
Das Leben in der Stadt ist aufregender als auf dem Land. — Life in the city is more exciting than in the countryside.

Key Fact

Use so...wie to say “as...as”: Meine Stadt ist nicht so groß wie London. (My town is not as big as London.) Use genauso...wie for “just as...as”: Das Dorf ist genauso schön wie die Stadt. (The village is just as beautiful as the city.)

In der Stadt gibt es mehr Geschäfte und Restaurants. — In the city there are more shops and restaurants.
Auf dem Land ist die Luft sauberer. — In the countryside the air is cleaner.
Die Stadt hat bessere Verkehrsverbindungen. — The city has better transport connections.
Das Landleben ist gesünder aber langweiliger. — Country life is healthier but more boring.
Ich möchte lieber in der Stadt wohnen, weil es mehr zu tun gibt. — I would prefer to live in the city because there is more to do.

Where You Would Like to Live

Use the Konjunktiv (conditional) to talk about your ideal area:

Ich möchte in einer großen Stadt wohnen. — I would like to live in a big city.
Ich würde gern am Meer wohnen. — I would like to live by the sea.
Meine Traumstadt wäre modern und lebhaft. — My dream town would be modern and lively.
Wenn ich reich wäre, würde ich in einem großen Haus auf dem Land wohnen. — If I were rich, I would live in a big house in the countryside.

Es gibt zu viel Verkehr. — There is too much traffic.
Es gibt nicht genug für junge Leute. — There is not enough for young people.
Die Busse fahren nicht oft genug. — The buses don’t run often enough.
Es gibt zu viel Lärm. — There is too much noise.
Es gibt Probleme mit Müll. — There are problems with rubbish/litter.
Die Mieten sind zu teuer. — The rents are too expensive.

Beziehungen und Zukunftspläne — Relationships and Future Plans

The AQA GCSE German exam expects you to discuss relationships, marriage, and future plans. This includes understanding different types of partnerships, giving opinions for and against marriage, and using the Konjunktiv (conditional tense) to talk about what you would like to do in the future. This is a higher-level topic that appears in both Foundation and Higher tier papers.

die Hochzeit — the wedding. Die Hochzeit wäre ein Zeichen der Liebe. (The wedding would be a sign of love.)
die Ehe — marriage/matrimony. Die Ehe ist Tradition.
heiraten — to get married. Ich möchte in zehn Jahren heiraten. (I would like to get married in ten years.)
die zivile Partnerschaft — civil partnership
die Feier — celebration
zusammenwohnen — to live together. Ich möchte mit meinem Partner zusammenwohnen.
allein wohnen — to live alone
ein Haus kaufen — to buy a house
Kinder haben — to have children
keine Kinder haben — to not have children
ledig bleiben — to stay single

Vorteile und Nachteile der Ehe — Pros and Cons of Marriage

The exam often asks you to discuss different viewpoints on marriage. Being able to argue both sides demonstrates the balanced language that earns top marks.

Es ist romantisch. — It is romantic.
Es ist gut für die Familie. — It is good for the family.
Es ist Tradition. — It is tradition.
Die Ehe ist in meiner Religion wichtig. — Marriage is important in my religion.
Es ist mir wichtig. — It is important to me.
Es ist ein Zeichen der Liebe. — It is a sign of love.
Es ist eine schöne Feier. — It is a beautiful celebration.
Man kann mit Familie und Freunden feiern. — You can celebrate with family and friends.

Es kostet zu viel. — It costs too much.
Es ist eine Geldverschwendung. — It is a waste of money.
Es ist langweilig. — It is boring.
Es ist nur ein Blatt Papier. — It is only a piece of paper.
Liebe ist wichtiger als eine Feier. — Love is more important than a celebration.
Man kann ohne Ehe glücklich sein. — You can be happy without marriage.
Viele Menschen werden geschieden. — Many people get divorced.
Ich möchte unabhängig bleiben. — I would like to stay independent.

Key Fact

To give a balanced argument in writing, use these discourse markers: Einerseits… (On one hand…), Andererseits… (On the other hand…), Außerdem… (Furthermore…), Jedoch… (However…), Trotzdem… (Nevertheless…). These are adverbial conjunctions — they go at the start of a sentence with the verb immediately after.

The Conditional Tense — Konjunktiv

The conditional tense describes hypothetical situations or future wishes. There are several conditional verbs in German, each paired with an infinitive that goes to the end of the sentence.

möchten — would like

The most common conditional verb at GCSE. It expresses what you would like to do:

  • ich möchte — I would like | er/sie möchte — he/she would like | wir/sie möchten — we/they would like

Word order: conjugation of möchten + other information + infinitive at the end:

  • Ich möchte in zehn Jahren heiraten. — I would like to get married in ten years.
  • Ich möchte keine Kinder haben. — I would not like to have children.
  • Ich möchte ein Haus kaufen. — I would like to buy a house.

würde + Infinitive — would

Würde (would) follows the same pattern as möchten — the infinitive goes to the end:

  • ich würde — I would | er/sie würde — he/she would | wir/sie würden — we/they would
  • Ich würde sagen, dass die Ehe wichtig ist. — I would say that marriage is important.

hätte / wäre — would have / would be

These two standalone conditional verbs do not need an infinitive:

  • hätte — would have: Mein idealer Partner hätte braune Haare. (My ideal partner would have brown hair.)
  • wäre — would be: Meine ideale Partnerin wäre geduldig. (My ideal partner would be patient.)

sollte / müsste — should / must

These conditional verbs also pair with an infinitive at the end:

  • Er sollte gute Kommunikation haben. — He should have good communication.
  • Sie müsste mich unterstützen. — She must support me.
Key Fact

Using the conditional tense is essential for reaching Grade 5+ on the AQA writing paper. The mark scheme requires “references to different time frames” for AO3. The conditional counts as a separate time frame alongside present, past and future. Even one or two conditional sentences can lift your grade.

Describing an Ideal Partner

Combining conditional verbs with personality and appearance vocabulary lets you describe an ideal partner:

  • Mein idealer Partner wäre groß und sportlich.
  • Meine ideale Partnerin hätte blonde Haare und blaue Augen.
  • Er würde mir immer zuhören. — He would always listen to me.
  • Sie sollte ehrlich und unabhängig sein. — She should be honest and independent.

Here is a model answer (WAGOLL — What A Good One Looks Like) covering three time frames:

In meiner Familie gibt es meinen Vater, der Paul heißt, meine Mutter, die Claudia heißt, und meine Geschwister. Ich verstehe mich gut mit meinen Eltern, weil sie lieb sind. Ich streite mich oft mit meinen Geschwistern, weil sie äußerst ärgerlich sind. [Present]

Meine ideale Partnerin hätte schwarze Haare und dunkelbraune Augen, weil das hübscher als blonde Haare ist. Meine ideale Partnerin wäre ein bisschen unabhängig und sehr freundlich. Jedoch wäre sie nie eifersüchtig. [Conditional]

Letztes Wochenende habe ich mit Freunden Fußball gespielt, weil das Spaß macht. Später haben wir Pizza gegessen und das war lecker. [Past]

This response covers all three bullet points, uses three time frames, includes weil clauses, comparatives (hübscher als), and adverbial conjunctions (Jedoch) — all features the mark scheme rewards.

Gesundes und ungesundes Essen

In this lesson you will learn to compare different foods and diets, use the Komparativ (comparative) to describe which foods are healthier or tastier, and justify your opinions using weil (because) and obwohl (although). You will also revise the past tense of food verbs so you can talk about what you ate and drank yesterday.

Weil und obwohl — Justifying Opinions

At GCSE, you must always justify your opinions. The two most important subordinating conjunctions for this are weil (because) and obwohl (although). Both send the verb to the end of the subordinate clause.

Key Fact

Memory trick: “Weil smells so vile that the verb runs a mile.” When you use weil or obwohl, the conjugated verb moves to the end of the clause. A comma always comes before weil or obwohl.

Here is how the word order changes:

Without conjunction: Ich esse gern Eis. Es ist lecker.
With weil: Ich esse gern Eis, weil es lecker ist. (I like eating ice cream because it is tasty.)
With obwohl: Ich trinke gern Cola, obwohl es ungesund ist. (I like drinking cola although it is unhealthy.)

More examples from the source material:
Ich esse nicht gern Fleisch, weil ich Vegetarier bin. (I don’t like eating meat because I am a vegetarian.)
Er isst gern Curry, obwohl es scharf schmeckt. (He likes eating curry although it tastes spicy.)

frisch — fresh • lecker — tasty • scharf — spicy • süß — sweet • gesund — healthy • ungesund — unhealthy • ekelhaft — disgusting • heiß — hot • kalt — cold • schnell — fast

Higher-tier vocabulary: die Ernährung (diet/nutrition) • das Gericht (dish) • das Protein (protein) • enthalten (to contain): Obst enthält Vitamine. (Fruit contains vitamins.)

Der Komparativ — Comparing Foods

The comparative is used to compare two things. In German, forming the comparative is simpler than in English — you always add –er to the adjective. You never use mehr (more) before the adjective.

Regular comparatives:
lecker → leckerer (tastier) • schnell → schneller (faster) • frisch → frischer (fresher) • süß → süßer (sweeter)

Key Fact

Most monosyllabic adjectives gain an umlaut in the comparative:
warm → wärmer • kalt → kälter • gesund → gesünder • scharf → schärfer
The word gut (good) is completely irregular: gut → besser (better) — just like English!

Use als (than) after the comparative to compare two items:

Obst ist gesünder als Kuchen. (Fruit is healthier than cake.)
Fisch ist frischer als Fastfood. (Fish is fresher than fast food.)
Kuchen ist süßer als Brot. (Cake is sweeter than bread.)
Wurst ist ungesünder als Gemüse. (Sausage is unhealthier than vegetables.)

For top marks, combine comparatives with weil or obwohl:
Ich esse gern Kuchen, weil es süßer als Brot ist. (I like eating cake because it is sweeter than bread.)
Ich esse lieber Hähnchen, weil es leckerer als Fisch ist. (I prefer eating chicken because it is tastier than fish.)
Notice that the verb ist still goes to the end after weil, even when there is a comparative + als phrase.

The Past Tense with Food Verbs

To talk about what you ate and drank yesterday (gestern), you need the Perfekt (perfect tense). Most food verbs use haben as the auxiliary verb. The past participle goes to the end of the sentence.

Key past participles for food:
essen → gegessen (ate) • trinken → getrunken (drank) • bestellen → bestellt (ordered) • kochen → gekocht (cooked) • finden → gefunden (found)

Gestern habe ich Pizza gegessen. (Yesterday I ate pizza.)
Ich habe Kaffee getrunken. (I drank coffee.)
Wir haben im Restaurant Fisch bestellt. (We ordered fish in the restaurant.)
Sie hat das Abendessen gekocht. (She cooked dinner.)
Ich habe es sehr lecker gefunden. (I found it very tasty.)

The word order follows the “hamburger method”: conjugated haben goes in position 2, the past participle goes at the very end, and everything else fills the middle.

Key Fact

In the exam, using three tenses (present, past and future) shows range and boosts your mark. A typical paragraph might say: Heute esse ich Obst (present), gestern habe ich Kuchen gegessen (past), and morgen werde ich Gemüse essen (future).

In listening and reading tasks, you need to identify whether someone is talking about now or the past. Look/listen for these clues:
Present: heute (today), ich esse, ich trinke
Past: gestern (yesterday), ich habe … gegessen, ich habe … getrunken
The presence of habe/hat/haben plus a ge– word at the end signals the past tense.

Berühmte Leute und Vorbilder — Celebrity Culture and Role Models

The AQA GCSE German specification includes celebrity culture as part of Theme 2 (Popular Culture). You need to be able to discuss famous people, describe what they do, give opinions on their influence, and say whether you consider them Vorbilder (role models). This topic is excellent for demonstrating opinion phrases, conditional tense, and complex sentence structures in your writing and speaking exams.

Famous People from German-Speaking Countries

The exam may include references to well-known German, Austrian or Swiss figures. Knowing about some of them gives you content for writing and speaking responses.

Sportler/innen (Athletes): Sebastian Vettel — Formula 1 driver, born in Germany, lived in Switzerland. Jule Brand — German women’s football player. Mesut Özil — German footballer of Turkish heritage.

Schauspieler/innen und Models (Actors and Models): Michael Fassbender — German-Irish actor. Heidi Klum — German-American supermodel and TV presenter.

Musiker/innen (Musicians): Beethoven — one of the greatest classical composers, born in Bonn. Nena — famous for “99 Luftballons.” Rammstein — globally famous rock band from Berlin.

Example: Sebastian Vettel ist in Deutschland geboren und wohnt jetzt in der Schweiz. Er ist ein berühmter Rennfahrer und ein Vorbild für viele junge Leute.

Describing Celebrities

To describe a celebrity, you need vocabulary for appearance, personality and achievements. Combine what you learned in the identity unit with new opinion phrases:

Appearance: Er/Sie hat braune Haare und blaue Augen. Er/Sie ist groß und sportlich. Personality: Er/Sie ist freundlich, großzügig, ehrlich, erfolgreich. Achievements: Er/Sie hat viele Preise gewonnen. Er/Sie ist weltweit berühmt.

Key Fact

Key adjectives for describing celebrities: berühmt (famous), erfolgreich (successful), talentiert (talented), inspirierend (inspiring), großzügig (generous), ehrgeizig (ambitious), verantwortlich (responsible), einflussreich (influential).

Opinions on Celebrity Influence

The exam tests whether you can give and justify Meinungen (opinions) about celebrity culture. You should be able to argue both for and against celebrities as role models.

Prominente können gute Vorbilder sein, weil sie hart arbeiten und zeigen, dass man Erfolg haben kann. (Celebrities can be good role models because they work hard and show that you can be successful.)

Viele Prominente setzen sich für wohltätige Zwecke ein und spenden viel Geld. (Many celebrities support charitable causes and donate a lot of money.) Sie inspirieren junge Leute, ihre Träume zu verfolgen. (They inspire young people to follow their dreams.)

Manche Prominente sind kein gutes Vorbild, weil sie einen unrealistischen Lebensstil zeigen. (Some celebrities are not a good role model because they show an unrealistic lifestyle.)

Junge Leute vergleichen sich oft mit Prominenten und das kann zu niedrigem Selbstwertgefühl führen. (Young people often compare themselves with celebrities and that can lead to low self-esteem.) Es gibt zu viel Druck, perfekt auszusehen. (There is too much pressure to look perfect.)

Using the Conditional Tense

The Konjunktiv II (conditional tense) is very useful for discussing celebrities and role models. It lets you talk about what you would do, who you would like to meet, and hypothetical situations.

Key Fact

Key conditional forms: Ich würde gern … treffen (I would like to meet …). Ich wäre gern berühmt (I would like to be famous). Er/Sie würde … (He/She would …). Ich möchte … werden (I would like to become …). The conditional shows the examiner you can use complex grammar beyond basic tenses.

Example paragraph: Wenn ich eine berühmte Person treffen könnte, würde ich Sebastian Vettel wählen. Ich bewundere ihn, weil er nicht nur ein fantastischer Rennfahrer ist, sondern auch viel für die Umwelt tut. Er ist ein gutes Vorbild, weil er zeigt, dass Erfolg und Verantwortung zusammengehören.

Advanced Opinion Structures

Push your answers into the higher mark bands with these sophisticated structures:

Einerseits … andererseits … — On the one hand … on the other hand … Ich bin der Meinung, dass … — I am of the opinion that … Obwohl …, finde ich … — Although …, I find … Nicht nur … sondern auch … — Not only … but also …

Key Fact

Using einerseits … andererseits (on the one hand … on the other hand) shows the examiner you can present a balanced argument. Example: Einerseits sind Prominente inspirierend, andererseits zeigen sie oft einen unrealistischen Lebensstil.

My Town and Local Area

  • Ich möchte keine Kinder haben. — I would not like to have children.
  • Ich möchte ein Haus kaufen. — I would like to buy a house.

würde + Infinitive — would

Würde (would) follows the same pattern as möchten — the infinitive goes to the end:

  • ich würde — I would | er/sie würde — he/she would | wir/sie würden — we/they would
  • Ich würde sagen, dass die Ehe wichtig ist. — I would say that marriage is important.

hätte / wäre — would have / would be

These two standalone conditional verbs do not need an infinitive:

  • hätte — would have: Mein idealer Partner hätte braune Haare. (My ideal partner would have brown hair.)
  • wäre — would be: Meine ideale Partnerin wäre geduldig. (My ideal partner would be patient.)

sollte / müsste — should / must

These conditional verbs also pair with an infinitive at the end:

  • Er sollte gute Kommunikation haben. — He should have good communication.
  • Sie müsste mich unterstützen. — She must support me.
Key Fact

Using the conditional tense is essential for reaching Grade 5+ on the AQA writing paper. The mark scheme requires “references to different time frames” for AO3. The conditional counts as a separate time frame alongside present, past and future. Even one or two conditional sentences can lift your grade.

Describing an Ideal Partner

Combining conditional verbs with personality and appearance vocabulary lets you describe an ideal partner:

  • Mein idealer Partner wäre groß und sportlich.
  • Meine ideale Partnerin hätte blonde Haare und blaue Augen.
  • Er würde mir immer zuhören. — He would always listen to me.
  • Sie sollte ehrlich und unabhängig sein. — She should be honest and independent.

Here is a model answer (WAGOLL — What A Good One Looks Like) covering three time frames:

In meiner Familie gibt es meinen Vater, der Paul heißt, meine Mutter, die Claudia heißt, und meine Geschwister. Ich verstehe mich gut mit meinen Eltern, weil sie lieb sind. Ich streite mich oft mit meinen Geschwistern, weil sie äußerst ärgerlich sind. [Present]

Meine ideale Partnerin hätte schwarze Haare und dunkelbraune Augen, weil das hübscher als blonde Haare ist. Meine ideale Partnerin wäre ein bisschen unabhängig und sehr freundlich. Jedoch wäre sie nie eifersüchtig. [Conditional]

Letztes Wochenende habe ich mit Freunden Fußball gespielt, weil das Spaß macht. Später haben wir Pizza gegessen und das war lecker. [Past]

This response covers all three bullet points, uses three time frames, includes weil clauses, comparatives (hübscher als), and adverbial conjunctions (Jedoch) — all features the mark scheme rewards.

Gesundes und ungesundes Essen

In this lesson you will learn to compare different foods and diets, use the Komparativ (comparative) to describe which foods are healthier or tastier, and justify your opinions using weil (because) and obwohl (although). You will also revise the past tense of food verbs so you can talk about what you ate and drank yesterday.

Weil und obwohl — Justifying Opinions

At GCSE, you must always justify your opinions. The two most important subordinating conjunctions for this are weil (because) and obwohl (although). Both send the verb to the end of the subordinate clause.

Key Fact

Memory trick: “Weil smells so vile that the verb runs a mile.” When you use weil or obwohl, the conjugated verb moves to the end of the clause. A comma always comes before weil or obwohl.

Here is how the word order changes:

Without conjunction: Ich esse gern Eis. Es ist lecker.
With weil: Ich esse gern Eis, weil es lecker ist. (I like eating ice cream because it is tasty.)
With obwohl: Ich trinke gern Cola, obwohl es ungesund ist. (I like drinking cola although it is unhealthy.)

More examples from the source material:
Ich esse nicht gern Fleisch, weil ich Vegetarier bin. (I don’t like eating meat because I am a vegetarian.)
Er isst gern Curry, obwohl es scharf schmeckt. (He likes eating curry although it tastes spicy.)

frisch — fresh • lecker — tasty • scharf — spicy • süß — sweet • gesund — healthy • ungesund — unhealthy • ekelhaft — disgusting • heiß — hot • kalt — cold • schnell — fast

Higher-tier vocabulary: die Ernährung (diet/nutrition) • das Gericht (dish) • das Protein (protein) • enthalten (to contain): Obst enthält Vitamine. (Fruit contains vitamins.)

Der Komparativ — Comparing Foods

The comparative is used to compare two things. In German, forming the comparative is simpler than in English — you always add –er to the adjective. You never use mehr (more) before the adjective.

Regular comparatives:
lecker → leckerer (tastier) • schnell → schneller (faster) • frisch → frischer (fresher) • süß → süßer (sweeter)

Key Fact

Most monosyllabic adjectives gain an umlaut in the comparative:
warm → wärmer • kalt → kälter • gesund → gesünder • scharf → schärfer
The word gut (good) is completely irregular: gut → besser (better) — just like English!

Use als (than) after the comparative to compare two items:

Obst ist gesünder als Kuchen. (Fruit is healthier than cake.)
Fisch ist frischer als Fastfood. (Fish is fresher than fast food.)
Kuchen ist süßer als Brot. (Cake is sweeter than bread.)
Wurst ist ungesünder als Gemüse. (Sausage is unhealthier than vegetables.)

For top marks, combine comparatives with weil or obwohl:
Ich esse gern Kuchen, weil es süßer als Brot ist. (I like eating cake because it is sweeter than bread.)
Ich esse lieber Hähnchen, weil es leckerer als Fisch ist. (I prefer eating chicken because it is tastier than fish.)
Notice that the verb ist still goes to the end after weil, even when there is a comparative + als phrase.

The Past Tense with Food Verbs

To talk about what you ate and drank yesterday (gestern), you need the Perfekt (perfect tense). Most food verbs use haben as the auxiliary verb. The past participle goes to the end of the sentence.

Key past participles for food:
essen → gegessen (ate) • trinken → getrunken (drank) • bestellen → bestellt (ordered) • kochen → gekocht (cooked) • finden → gefunden (found)

Gestern habe ich Pizza gegessen. (Yesterday I ate pizza.)
Ich habe Kaffee getrunken. (I drank coffee.)
Wir haben im Restaurant Fisch bestellt. (We ordered fish in the restaurant.)
Sie hat das Abendessen gekocht. (She cooked dinner.)
Ich habe es sehr lecker gefunden. (I found it very tasty.)

The word order follows the “hamburger method”: conjugated haben goes in position 2, the past participle goes at the very end, and everything else fills the middle.

Key Fact

In the exam, using three tenses (present, past and future) shows range and boosts your mark. A typical paragraph might say: Heute esse ich Obst (present), gestern habe ich Kuchen gegessen (past), and morgen werde ich Gemüse essen (future).

In listening and reading tasks, you need to identify whether someone is talking about now or the past. Look/listen for these clues:
Present: heute (today), ich esse, ich trinke
Past: gestern (yesterday), ich habe … gegessen, ich habe … getrunken
The presence of habe/hat/haben plus a ge– word at the end signals the past tense.

Berühmte Leute und Vorbilder — Celebrity Culture and Role Models

The AQA GCSE German specification includes celebrity culture as part of Theme 2 (Popular Culture). You need to be able to discuss famous people, describe what they do, give opinions on their influence, and say whether you consider them Vorbilder (role models). This topic is excellent for demonstrating opinion phrases, conditional tense, and complex sentence structures in your writing and speaking exams.

Famous People from German-Speaking Countries

The exam may include references to well-known German, Austrian or Swiss figures. Knowing about some of them gives you content for writing and speaking responses.

Sportler/innen (Athletes): Sebastian Vettel — Formula 1 driver, born in Germany, lived in Switzerland. Jule Brand — German women’s football player. Mesut Özil — German footballer of Turkish heritage.

Schauspieler/innen und Models (Actors and Models): Michael Fassbender — German-Irish actor. Heidi Klum — German-American supermodel and TV presenter.

Musiker/innen (Musicians): Beethoven — one of the greatest classical composers, born in Bonn. Nena — famous for “99 Luftballons.” Rammstein — globally famous rock band from Berlin.

Example: Sebastian Vettel ist in Deutschland geboren und wohnt jetzt in der Schweiz. Er ist ein berühmter Rennfahrer und ein Vorbild für viele junge Leute.

Describing Celebrities

To describe a celebrity, you need vocabulary for appearance, personality and achievements. Combine what you learned in the identity unit with new opinion phrases:

Appearance: Er/Sie hat braune Haare und blaue Augen. Er/Sie ist groß und sportlich. Personality: Er/Sie ist freundlich, großzügig, ehrlich, erfolgreich. Achievements: Er/Sie hat viele Preise gewonnen. Er/Sie ist weltweit berühmt.

Key Fact

Key adjectives for describing celebrities: berühmt (famous), erfolgreich (successful), talentiert (talented), inspirierend (inspiring), großzügig (generous), ehrgeizig (ambitious), verantwortlich (responsible), einflussreich (influential).

Opinions on Celebrity Influence

The exam tests whether you can give and justify Meinungen (opinions) about celebrity culture. You should be able to argue both for and against celebrities as role models.

Prominente können gute Vorbilder sein, weil sie hart arbeiten und zeigen, dass man Erfolg haben kann. (Celebrities can be good role models because they work hard and show that you can be successful.)

Viele Prominente setzen sich für wohltätige Zwecke ein und spenden viel Geld. (Many celebrities support charitable causes and donate a lot of money.) Sie inspirieren junge Leute, ihre Träume zu verfolgen. (They inspire young people to follow their dreams.)

Manche Prominente sind kein gutes Vorbild, weil sie einen unrealistischen Lebensstil zeigen. (Some celebrities are not a good role model because they show an unrealistic lifestyle.)

Junge Leute vergleichen sich oft mit Prominenten und das kann zu niedrigem Selbstwertgefühl führen. (Young people often compare themselves with celebrities and that can lead to low self-esteem.) Es gibt zu viel Druck, perfekt auszusehen. (There is too much pressure to look perfect.)

Using the Conditional Tense

The Konjunktiv II (conditional tense) is very useful for discussing celebrities and role models. It lets you talk about what you would do, who you would like to meet, and hypothetical situations.

Key Fact

Key conditional forms: Ich würde gern … treffen (I would like to meet …). Ich wäre gern berühmt (I would like to be famous). Er/Sie würde … (He/She would …). Ich möchte … werden (I would like to become …). The conditional shows the examiner you can use complex grammar beyond basic tenses.

Example paragraph: Wenn ich eine berühmte Person treffen könnte, würde ich Sebastian Vettel wählen. Ich bewundere ihn, weil er nicht nur ein fantastischer Rennfahrer ist, sondern auch viel für die Umwelt tut. Er ist ein gutes Vorbild, weil er zeigt, dass Erfolg und Verantwortung zusammengehören.

Advanced Opinion Structures

Push your answers into the higher mark bands with these sophisticated structures:

Einerseits … andererseits … — On the one hand … on the other hand … Ich bin der Meinung, dass … — I am of the opinion that … Obwohl …, finde ich … — Although …, I find … Nicht nur … sondern auch … — Not only … but also …

Key Fact

Using einerseits … andererseits (on the one hand … on the other hand) shows the examiner you can present a balanced argument. Example: Einerseits sind Prominente inspirierend, andererseits zeigen sie oft einen unrealistischen Lebensstil.

Jewish Belief in One G-d

At the heart of Judaism is monotheism — the belief in one God and one God alone. The Torah opens with the declaration that G-d created the heavens and the earth, establishing from the first verse that all existence depends on this one creator. Genesis 1:3–5 describes G-d bringing light into being through speech alone, conveying an unlimited creative power that requires no materials or assistance. Exodus 20:1–17, the Ten Commandments, begins with G-d identifying himself as the God who brought Israel out of Egypt — linking belief in one God to the history of a real community.

Jewish belief in G-d is not abstract. G-d is understood as omnipotent (all-powerful), omnipresent (present everywhere), and omnibenevolent (all-loving and good). G-d is also eternal, existing outside time and not subject to change or decay. These qualities distinguish the Jewish God from the gods of surrounding ancient peoples, who were often depicted as limited, rivalrous, or morally flawed.

Key Fact

The Shema is the most important prayer in Judaism, drawn from Deuteronomy 6:4. It declares that G-d is one — a statement of absolute monotheism. Observant Jews recite it in the morning and the evening.

G-d as Transcendent, Merciful, and Judge

Judaism teaches that G-d is transcendent — wholly beyond the created order, not contained within it. Isaiah 55:8–9 expresses this powerfully, declaring that G-d’s thoughts and ways are higher than human thoughts and ways, as the heavens are higher than the earth. This means G-d cannot be fully comprehended by human reason alone, and visual representations of G-d are forbidden.

Yet G-d is also personal and relational. Jewish tradition emphasises G-d’s mercy (rachamim) alongside justice. G-d forgives those who genuinely repent, and the annual cycle of festivals includes Rosh Hashanah (the Day of Judgement) and Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement), when Jews seek forgiveness. G-d as eternal judge means that human moral choices have ultimate significance — G-d rewards the righteous and punishes wrongdoing, though divine mercy always accompanies divine justice in Jewish theology.

Because G-d is so far beyond human understanding, Jewish tradition exercises great care with the divine name. Many observant Jews write “G-d” instead of the full word, and the four Hebrew letters of the divine name (the Tetragrammaton, YHWH) are not pronounced as written. When reading the Torah aloud, Jews substitute “Adonai” (Lord) for the written name.

The synagogue serves four functions in Jewish life: prayer, study, celebration, and assembly. It is not considered sacred in the way a Temple was sacred; rather, it is the community that makes the place holy. This means synagogues vary enormously in design, from ornate Victorian buildings to converted terraced houses.

Key features of the synagogue include: the aron hakodesh (the ark), a cabinet at the front wall containing the Torah scrolls; the ner tamid (the eternal light), a lamp that burns continuously above or in front of the ark, representing G-d’s constant presence; the bimah, a raised platform from which the Torah is read; and displayed text of the Ten Commandments, often above the ark. Seating arrangements differ between traditions: in Orthodox synagogues, men and women sit separately; in Reform and Liberal synagogues, they sit together.

Orthodox, Reform, and Liberal Judaism differ significantly in synagogue practice. In Orthodox synagogues, services are conducted primarily in Hebrew, led by a male rabbi, and women do not read from the Torah in the main service. Reform and Liberal synagogues use more English in services, ordain female rabbis, and allow mixed seating. These differences reflect wider debates about how Jewish law (halakha) should be interpreted in the modern world.

The Home as a Place of Worship

In Jewish life, the home is as important as the synagogue. The philosopher Abraham Joshua Heschel described the Sabbath as a “cathedral in time” — and much of Jewish religious life is practised within the family home rather than in a communal building. This emphasis on domestic faith means that Jewish identity is transmitted across generations primarily through family practice.

A visible sign of this is the mezuzah, a small case attached to the doorpost of Jewish homes (and often of every room), containing a handwritten parchment with verses from Deuteronomy including the Shema. Touching the mezuzah and kissing one’s fingers upon entering and leaving reminds the family of G-d’s presence in everyday life.

The home is especially central to Shabbat observance. Shabbat begins at sunset on Friday and ends at nightfall on Saturday, following the commandment in Exodus 20:8–10 to remember the Sabbath and keep it holy. The family lights candles, says blessings over wine (kiddush) and bread (challah), and abstains from creative work. Shabbat creates a weekly rhythm of rest that re-centres Jewish life on G-d. The challenges of observing Shabbat fully — not driving, not using electronic devices, not cooking — are real in modern Britain, and different families and communities navigate them differently.

Key Fact

The mezuzah (doorpost case) and Shabbat candles are two key ways Jewish domestic space expresses faith. Observing Shabbat at home is commanded in Exodus 20:8–10: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.”

Because G-d is transcendent — entirely beyond the material world — Judaism forbids any artistic representation of G-d. Images or statues would reduce the infinite to something finite and manageable, which would misrepresent G-d’s true nature. This shapes synagogue decoration: Hebrew calligraphy, geometric patterns, and symbolic imagery replace figurative art. The Shema displayed in beautiful script makes language the medium for divine encounter.

The kippah (skullcap) worn by many Jewish men is a visible reminder that G-d is above, watching over the person’s actions. The tallit (prayer shawl) is worn during morning prayer; its fringes (tzitzit) remind the wearer of all 613 commandments. These practices embed awareness of G-d’s presence into daily bodily routine.
